chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting ready to sell to the government

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Registering in SAM.gov and getting a UEI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Gather what you need and register your business in SAM.gov yourself, for free.
This lesson builds toward: Given your business's legal name, address, EIN and bank details, you will register your business in SAM.gov yourself and get a UEI, for free, renewing every 365 days and ignoring paid registration offers.
SAM.gov (the System for Award Management) is the US government's official site for doing business with federal agencies. To bid on and win federal contracts, your business must be registered there. Registration gives you a Unique Entity ID (UEI), a 12-character code made of letters and numbers that identifies your business.
You can request only a UEI without full registration, but with a UEI alone you cannot apply directly for federal awards. For contracts, complete the full registration. You must renew it every 365 days to keep it active.
Registering in SAM.gov is free. Some companies send official-looking emails or letters offering to register or renew you for a fee, or warn that your registration is about to expire. You never have to pay them. Register only at sam.gov, and get free help from an APEX Accelerator if you are stuck.
Before you start, gather your legal business name and physical address exactly as the IRS has them, your Employer Identification Number (EIN) or tax ID, and bank details for payments. Type these only into SAM.gov itself, never into an AI tool or an email.
Step by step:
- Gather your legal business name, physical address, EIN and bank details.
- Go to sam.gov and create a login.
- Choose to register your entity, not just get a UEI.
- Answer every section; the business name and address must match IRS records.
- Write down your UEI and the date your registration expires.
- Set a reminder to renew before 365 days.
Words to know:
- SAM.gov: the System for Award Management, the federal site where businesses register to sell to the government.
- UEI: Unique Entity ID: the 12-character code that identifies your business to the government.
- EIN: Employer Identification Number: your business's tax ID from the IRS.
- APEX Accelerator: a free counseling center that helps businesses sell to the government.
Official sources:
- SAM.gov: Entity registration
- SBA: Basic requirements for government contracting
Try it now: Make a SAM.gov registration checklist for your business: legal name, physical address, EIN, bank details, contact person. Mark which you already have. If you are already registered, look up your expiration date and set a renewal reminder.
You can now get ready for and complete a free SAM.gov registration, explain what a UEI is, and spot paid registration scams.

check.q: What must your legal name and address in SAM.gov match?
options: What the IRS has for your business
check.why: Your legal name and address must match the IRS exactly.

check.q: You are stuck on a SAM.gov registration step. Where can you get free help?
options: A company that emailed you offering help for $300
An AI tool, by pasting in your bank details
check.why: APEX Accelerators give free help; you never have to pay to register.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Choosing NAICS codes and checking your size
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick a primary NAICS code and check whether your business counts as small for it.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Census NAICS page and SBA's Size Standards Tool, you will choose a primary NAICS code and check whether your business counts as small for it, with the code matching your main service.
NAICS codes (North American Industry Classification System) sort businesses by what they sell. Each government contract is given one NAICS code, and buyers search for businesses by code. For example, there are codes for janitorial services, commercial printing and computer systems design.
Look up codes on the US Census Bureau's NAICS page (census.gov/naics) by typing words that describe your work. Choose one primary code for your main service and add others for other things you sell.
Each NAICS code has a size standard: the largest a business can be and still count as small for that code, measured by yearly receipts or number of employees. Most manufacturers with 500 or fewer employees and most non-manufacturers averaging under $7.5 million a year count as small, but it varies. Check yours with SBA's Size Standards Tool.
Being small for a code lets you compete for contracts set aside for small businesses under that code.
Step by step:
- List what you sell in plain words.
- Search census.gov/naics for matching codes.
- Pick one primary code and two or three others.
- Check each code with SBA's Size Standards Tool.
- Add the codes to your SAM.gov registration.
Words to know:
- NAICS code: a number that describes the kind of business you are.
- Primary NAICS code: the code for your main product or service.
- Size standard: the largest a business can be and still count as small for a NAICS code.
- Set-aside: a contract only certain businesses, such as small businesses, can compete for.
Official sources:
- SBA: Size standards
- US Census Bureau: NAICS
Try it now: Search census.gov/naics for your main service and write down your primary NAICS code and two more. Then check one of them in SBA's Size Standards Tool and write whether your business counts as small.
You can now choose NAICS codes for your business and check whether you count as small for each one.

check.q: How many NAICS codes is each government contract given?
options: As many as the bidder wants
check.why: Each contract is given one NAICS code, and buyers search by code.

check.q: You run a cleaning company that also sells some supplies. How do you choose codes?
options: Skip codes; buyers search by name
Choose cleaning as the primary code and add others for what else you sell
check.why: Choose one primary code for your main service and add others for other things you sell.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: SBA and California certifications
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Decide which federal and California certifications your business might qualify for.
This lesson builds toward: Given the basic rules for SBA and California certifications, you will identify which certifications your business might qualify for and where to apply, naming the right site for each one.
Certifications let you compete for contracts reserved for certain small businesses. Federal certifications are applied for at certifications.sba.gov. Each has rules; these are the basics, so check SBA's pages for the full list.
8(a) Business Development: for small businesses at least 51% owned and controlled by socially and economically disadvantaged US citizens, with personal net worth, income and asset limits, usually two years in business, and a one-time program of up to nine years. HUBZone: your main office is in a HUBZone (Historically Underutilized Business Zone) and at least 35% of employees live in one. Women-Owned Small Business (WOSB): at least 51% owned and controlled by women who are US citizens; the government aims to give 5% of contract dollars to WOSBs. Veteran-owned (VOSB) and service-disabled veteran-owned (SDVOSB): certified by SBA's VetCert program since 2023.
California has its own certifications from the Department of General Services' Office of Small Business and DVBE Services, applied for in Cal eProcure. Small Business (SB): independently owned, main office in California, and, with affiliates, 100 or fewer employees and average yearly gross receipts of $19 million or less (or a manufacturer with 100 or fewer employees). Disabled Veteran Business Enterprise (DVBE): at least 51% owned and managed by disabled veterans with a service-connected disability of at least 10%.
Many cities, counties and school districts honor state certifications too. Ask an APEX Accelerator which ones fit you.
Words to know:
- 8(a): an SBA program for small businesses owned by socially and economically disadvantaged people.
- HUBZone: a Historically Underutilized Business Zone; businesses there can get contracting help.
- WOSB: Women-Owned Small Business.
- SDVOSB: Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business.
- DVBE: Disabled Veteran Business Enterprise, a California certification.
Official sources:
- SBA: 8(a) Business Development program
- SBA: HUBZone program
- SBA: Women-Owned Small Business program
- SBA: Veteran contracting assistance (VetCert)
- California DGS: Apply for Small Business and DVBE certification
Try it now: Make a table of the six certifications in this lesson (8(a), HUBZone, WOSB, VOSB or SDVOSB, California SB, California DVBE). For each, write yes, maybe or no for your business, and the one rule that decides it. Circle the one you will look into first.
You can now name the main SBA and California certifications, check which ones your business might qualify for, and know where to apply.

check.q: Where do you apply for federal SBA certifications?
options: A private website that charges a fee
check.why: Federal certifications are applied for at certifications.sba.gov.

check.q: You are a disabled veteran who owns a California business. Which state certification should you look into?
check.why: California's DVBE is for businesses at least 51% owned and managed by disabled veterans.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding opportunities
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Search SAM.gov and Cal eProcure for opportunities that match your NAICS codes and save the search.
This lesson builds toward: Using SAM.gov and Cal eProcure, you will find and save a search for opportunities that match your NAICS codes, so new matches come to your email.
Federal agencies post contract opportunities on SAM.gov. Search Contract Opportunities by your NAICS code, your state and the type of set-aside, such as small business, 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB or SDVOSB. Save your search so new matches come to your email.
California state agencies post bids on Cal eProcure (caleprocure.ca.gov). Register there, add keywords and UNSPSC product codes to your profile, and turn on notifications. Cal eProcure also shows what departments have bought before and at what prices, which helps you set your own.
You do not have to win a big contract first. Many small businesses start as subcontractors to larger prime contractors. California departments have SB/DVBE Advocates who help certified businesses, and APEX Accelerators help you find bids for free.
Look for opportunities that match what you already do well, in an area you can serve, at a size you can handle.
Step by step:
- On SAM.gov, search Contract Opportunities by your NAICS code and state.
- Filter by the set-asides you qualify for.
- Save the search so new matches come by email.
- Register on Cal eProcure and add keywords and UNSPSC codes for notifications.
- Contact an APEX Accelerator or SB/DVBE Advocate for leads.
Words to know:
- Contract opportunity: a posted notice that the government wants to buy something.
- Prime contractor: the business that holds the contract with the government.
- Subcontractor: a business hired by the prime contractor to do part of the work.
- UNSPSC: a product and service code used by California's bidding system.
Official sources:
- SAM.gov
- California DGS: How to do business with the State of California
- Cal eProcure: Find bid opportunities
Try it now: Search SAM.gov Contract Opportunities using your primary NAICS code and your state. Write down two opportunities: the agency, what they want, the set-aside and the due date. Save the search.
You can now find federal and California contract opportunities that match your codes and set up alerts.

check.q: Where do California state agencies post bids?
check.why: California state agencies post bids on Cal eProcure.

check.q: You find a huge contract far outside your area that you could not handle. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to bid for you
Look for opportunities that match what you do well at a size you can handle
check.why: Look for work you do well, in an area you can serve, at a size you can handle.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reading a solicitation
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Read a solicitation's key parts and decide whether to bid.
This lesson builds toward: Given a solicitation, you will find its statement of work, instructions, evaluation criteria and due date, and decide whether to bid, answering every bid or no-bid question.
A solicitation is the government's request for offers. It may be called a Request for Quote (RFQ), Request for Proposal (RFP) or Invitation for Bid (IFB). They can be long, but you only need to find a few key parts first.
Find these: the statement of work (what they want done), the instructions (what to send and how), the evaluation criteria (how they will choose a winner, such as lowest price or best value), the due date and time, the deadline for questions, and the contracting officer's name. Also check for amendments, which are changes posted later.
Then decide bid or no bid. Ask: Can we do this work well? Do we meet every requirement, such as licenses, insurance and the set-aside? Can we deliver on time and at a price that still makes a profit? Do we have similar past work to show?
Missing one instruction, such as a page limit or a required form, can get an offer rejected. Make a checklist from the instructions and tick each item before you submit. An AI assistant can help you summarize a long public solicitation, but you must read the real instructions yourself.
Step by step:
- Find the statement of work, instructions and evaluation criteria.
- Write the due date and time, the questions deadline and the contracting officer.
- Check for amendments.
- Answer the four bid or no-bid questions.
- If you bid, turn the instructions into a checklist and tick every item.
Words to know:
- Solicitation: the government's request for offers, such as an RFQ, RFP or IFB.
- Statement of work: the part that says exactly what work is wanted.
- Evaluation criteria: how the government will choose the winner.
- Amendment: a change to a solicitation posted after it first comes out.
- Contracting officer: the government person with authority to sign the contract.
Try it now: Open one of the opportunities you found in the last lesson. Write down the statement of work in one sentence, the evaluation criteria, the due date and time, and the questions deadline. Then answer the four bid or no-bid questions and decide.
You can now find the key parts of a solicitation and make a clear bid or no-bid decision.

check.q: Which is another name for a solicitation?
check.why: A solicitation may be called an RFQ, RFP or IFB.

check.q: The instructions set a 10-page limit. What do you do?
options: Add it to your checklist and tick it before you submit
Ignore it; it is only a suggestion
check.why: Missing one instruction, such as a page limit, can get your offer rejected.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a capability statement
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page capability statement that tells a buyer what you do and how to reach you.
This lesson builds toward: For government buyers and prime contractors, you will write a one-page capability statement with core competencies, past performance, differentiators and company data, with no private numbers such as bank details or EIN.
A capability statement is a one-page summary of your business for government buyers and prime contractors. You send it when you meet buyers, at outreach events, and when you introduce yourself to a contracting officer or SB/DVBE Advocate.
It has four parts. Core competencies: what you do best, in short bullet points. Past performance: two or three jobs you have done, with the customer type, what you did and the result. Differentiators: what makes you different, such as speed, a special skill or local presence. Company data: legal name, UEI, CAGE code if you have one, NAICS codes, certifications, and contact details.
Keep it to one page, easy to scan, with your logo and contact at the top. Use the buyer's words from the statement of work when they fit. Make a version for each kind of buyer if you sell different services.
An AI assistant can help you shorten bullets or make them clearer. Do not paste in private numbers like your bank details or EIN; your UEI and NAICS codes are fine to show.
Step by step:
- Write three to five core competencies as short bullets.
- Add two or three past performance examples: customer type, work, result.
- Write two or three differentiators.
- Add company data: legal name, UEI, CAGE code, NAICS codes, certifications and contact.
- Fit it on one page and save it as a PDF.
Words to know:
- Capability statement: a one-page summary of your business for government buyers.
- Core competencies: the things your business does best.
- Past performance: work you have done before that shows you can deliver.
- Differentiator: something that makes your business different from others.
- CAGE code: a code that identifies businesses doing work for the government, assigned with SAM registration.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page capability statement with core competencies, past performance, differentiators and company data. Then find one real opportunity on SAM.gov or Cal eProcure that matches a NAICS code on your statement and write down its title and due date.
You can now write a one-page capability statement and match it to real government opportunities.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Core competencies Vague or missing, such as "we do everything". Short bullet points of what the business does best. Uses the buyer's words from a statement of work where they fit. Past performance No past jobs, or jobs without results. Two or three jobs with customer type, what was done and the result. Picks the jobs most like the work government buyers want. Differentiators Nothing that sets the business apart. States clearly what makes the business different. Backs each point with a fact from real work, such as speed or local presence. Company data Missing the UEI or NAICS codes, or shows bank details or EIN. Legal name, UEI, NAICS codes, certifications and contact details, with no private numbers. Primary NAICS code is checked against the size standard. Matching opportunity No opportunity found, or it does not match a NAICS code on the statement. One real opportunity on SAM.gov or Cal eProcure that matches a NAICS code on the statement. The search is saved and a bid or no-bid decision is written down. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How long should a capability statement be?
check.why: It is a one-page summary that is easy to scan.

check.q: You are writing your company data section. What do you leave out?
check.why: UEI and NAICS codes are fine to show; private numbers like bank details and EIN are not.
